summary: Describes version 3 of the Network File System protocol, so that people can write compatible implementations. It is an informational description, not an Internet standard.

plainLanguage.summary: NFS version 3 lets a client access files stored on a server by sending remote procedure calls. This specification describes the messages and procedures that compatible implementations use, including support for larger files and a way to make asynchronous writes durable.

how does nfs version 3 commit writes
subtitle: The NFS version 3 procedures for remote file access, larger files, and committing asynchronous writes.

tldr.problem: NFS version 2 had limits for file sizes and transfer behavior, and its synchronous writes could restrict write throughput.
tldr.mechanism: NFS version 3 keeps the RPC-based design, adds 64-bit file sizes and offsets, returns more attributes with operations, adds an ACCESS check, and supports asynchronous WRITE followed by COMMIT.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1813 is an Informational protocol description intended to help people build compatible implementations. The IESG note says the IETF is not involved in creating or maintaining it.

today: RFC 1813 is an Informational document published in June 1995, not an Internet Standards Track specification. Its IESG note says the IETF is not involved in creating or maintaining it.

sections.title: What the NFS Version 3 Specification Covers
sections.content:
NFS provides remote access to shared file systems. Version 3 uses Remote Procedure Call (RPC) and External Data Representation (XDR), so its protocol data can be represented consistently across machines and operating systems. The RFC defines the NFS procedures and also specifies the supporting MOUNT version 3 protocol.

The document's normative content is the description of RPC procedures, arguments, results, and their semantics. It also includes implementation discussion, plus an appendix describing the Network Lock Manager changes associated with NFS version 3. An IESG note states that the IETF is not involved in creating or maintaining this specification.
sections.plainLanguage: This document describes how an NFS client asks a server to access files. It defines the network procedures and data they exchange, while noting that it is not an IETF-maintained specification.

sections.title: A Stateless Server and Client Retries
sections.content:
The protocol assumes that a server does not need to keep client-specific state in order to work correctly. If a request or reply is lost, the client can time out and retry. Servers may keep non-critical state, such as read-ahead data, to improve performance, but losing that state must not prevent correct operation.

Retries can repeat an operation. The RFC describes a duplicate request cache that remembers the result of recent requests so the server can return the original result rather than perform a non-idempotent operation again. This cache reduces destructive duplicate effects but is not a complete guarantee: many servers keep it in memory, and a crash or network partition can make an old request appear new.
sections.plainLanguage: The server can recover without remembering every client interaction, and the client can retry when it does not receive an answer. A short-term cache helps prevent some repeated requests from performing an operation twice.

sections.title: Changes from Version 2
sections.content:
Version 3 widens file sizes and offsets to 64 bits and allows variable-length file handles up to 64 bytes. It relaxes artificial limits on transfer sizes and filename lengths, with server transfer guidance available through FSINFO.

To reduce extra calls, many operations return file attributes along with their results. ACCESS lets the client ask the server to check permissions. READDIRPLUS returns file handles and attributes with directory entries, while FSSTAT, FSINFO, and PATHCONF provide file-system information. MKNOD supports special files, and COMMIT supports asynchronous writes.
sections.plainLanguage: Version 3 supports larger files and file handles, and it returns more useful information with operations. New procedures let clients check access, read directory details, query file-system properties, and commit pending writes.

sections.title: Asynchronous Writes and COMMIT
sections.content:
A synchronous WRITE returns only after modified data is on stable storage. Version 3 also permits an UNSTABLE WRITE, where the server may reply before the data is durable. The client must keep that data available until it sends COMMIT or rewrites the data with a stable-write setting.

COMMIT asks the server to flush earlier asynchronous data and associated metadata to stable storage. The server returns a verifier. If a later WRITE or COMMIT returns an unexpected verifier, the client must retransmit its uncommitted data because the server may have lost it.
sections.plainLanguage: A client can ask the server to accept data before it has been made durable. The client later sends COMMIT, and must resend uncommitted data if the server's verifier indicates that the server instance changed.

sections.title: File Operations and Mounting
sections.content:
NFS version 3 provides procedures to read and write files, create or remove file-system objects, inspect attributes, and work with directories. LOOKUP resolves one pathname component at a time; the client builds the hierarchy by mounting remote directory trees. The MOUNT protocol lets a client attach a remote directory tree and lets the server restrict which clients may access exported file systems.

The service uses RPC program number 100003 and version 3. The RFC says it is normally supported over TCP and UDP on port 2049. It also describes authentication information carried with RPC calls and permission checks performed by the server.
sections.plainLanguage: The client uses individual procedures to find, read, write, and manage files. It combines one-component lookups and mounts to build the remote directory structure it presents to applications.

sections.title: Authentication and Protection
sections.content:
The RFC says implementations should address authentication, privacy, and data integrity because file data may be sensitive. NFS relies on authentication provided by RPC and assumes that privacy and integrity are supplied by lower layers where available.

RPC authentication flavors described include AUTH_NONE, AUTH_UNIX, AUTH_DES, and AUTH_KERB. AUTH_UNIX carries user and group identifiers. The other named flavors use encrypted authentication parameters. The client and server must agree on how user and group identities map between them.
sections.plainLanguage: NFS carries credentials with each remote call, and the server uses them to check permissions. The RFC leaves privacy and data integrity to underlying layers where those protections are available.
